Content:
We've shown that two sets have the same cardinality by finding a bijection between them. However, finding a bijection between two sets can be difficult. So, is there another way to show that two sets have the same cardinality?

Content:
To answer this, we take inspiration from a well-known property of the real numbers.

Content:
Recall that if [MATH: x\leq y] and [MATH: y\leq x] for real [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] then [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] must be equal. We can write this symbolically as follows:
[MATH: (x\leq y) \land (y\leq x) \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x = y]

Content:
As it turns out, this straightforward idea provides the key. So, let's start by thinking about what inequalities mean in the context of set cardinalities:

Content:
Consider the following sets:
[MATH: A = \{x,y,z\}, \qquad B = \{1,2,3,4\}]

Content:
For finite sets [MATH: A] and [MATH: B,] the notation [MATH: |A| < |B|] means that [MATH: A] contains fewer elements than [MATH: B.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c869467961ce62523b444df8378560bf]

Content:
As the image suggests, another way of thinking about the statement [MATH: |A| < |B|] is in terms of the function [MATH: f: A\rightarrow B] indicated by the arrows in the diagram.

Content:
- The function [MATH: f] is injective since no two distinct elements of [MATH: A] map to the same element of [MATH: B.] In other words, [MATH: f] is one-to-one.
- However, [MATH: f] is not surjective since the element [MATH: 4\in B] is not paired with any element of [MATH: A.]
- Since [MATH: f] is injective but not surjective, it's not bijective.

Content:
Moreover, it is impossible to find a bijective function that maps [MATH: A] onto [MATH: B,] although finding injective functions is easy. This leads us to our first definition:

Content:
> If there exists an injection [MATH: f:A \to B] but there is no bijection between [MATH: A] and [MATH: B,] we say that the cardinality of [MATH: A] is (strictly) smaller than the cardinality of [MATH: B.]
> [MATH: |A| < |B|]

Following similar lines, we can also define [MATH: |A|\leq |B|{:}]

Content:
> If there exists an injection [MATH: f:A \to B] that maps [MATH: A] into [MATH: B,] we write
> [MATH: |A| \leq |B|.]

We can illustrate [MATH: |A|\leq |B|] for two (possibly infinite) sets [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] as follows:

Content:
In previous lessons, we saw that the cardinality of the natural numbers is [MATH: |\mathbb N| = \aleph_0,] the cardinality of the reals is [MATH: |\mathbb R| = \mathfrak{c},] and that these two cardinalities are different. We're now able to state that
[MATH: |\mathbb N| < |\mathbb R|.]
To see why, note the following:

- It's easy to find an injective function [MATH: f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R.] For example [MATH: f(n) = n] is injective.
- However, Cantor's diagonal argument shows no bijection exists between [MATH: \mathbb N] and [MATH: \mathbb R].
- Therefore, by definition, we have [MATH: |\mathbb N| < |\mathbb R|,] i.e.,
[MATH: \aleph_0 < \mathfrak{c}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Recall that two sets [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] have the same cardinality if there exists a bijection from [MATH: A] onto [MATH: B.] In such cases, we write
[MATH: |A| = |B|.]

Content:
We've shown that two sets have the same cardinality by finding a bijection between them. However, finding a bijection between two sets can be difficult. So, is there another way to show that two sets have the same cardinality?

Content:
To answer this, we take inspiration from a well-known property of the real numbers.

Content:
Recall that if [MATH: x\leq y] and [MATH: y\leq x] for real [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] then [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] must be equal. We can write this symbolically as follows:
[MATH: (x\leq y) \land (y\leq x) \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x = y]

Content:
As it turns out, this straightforward idea provides the key. So, let's start by thinking about what inequalities mean in the context of set cardinalities:

Content:
Consider the following sets:
[MATH: A = \{x,y,z\}, \qquad B = \{1,2,3,4\}]

Content:
For finite sets [MATH: A] and [MATH: B,] the notation [MATH: |A| < |B|] means that [MATH: A] contains fewer elements than [MATH: B.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c869467961ce62523b444df8378560bf]

Content:
As the image suggests, another way of thinking about the statement [MATH: |A| < |B|] is in terms of the function [MATH: f: A\rightarrow B] indicated by the arrows in the diagram.

Content:
- The function [MATH: f] is injective since no two distinct elements of [MATH: A] map to the same element of [MATH: B.] In other words, [MATH: f] is one-to-one.
- However, [MATH: f] is not surjective since the element [MATH: 4\in B] is not paired with any element of [MATH: A.]
- Since [MATH: f] is injective but not surjective, it's not bijective.

Content:
Moreover, it is impossible to find a bijective function that maps [MATH: A] onto [MATH: B,] although finding injective functions is easy. This leads us to our first definition:

Content:
> If there exists an injection [MATH: f:A \to B] but there is no bijection between [MATH: A] and [MATH: B,] we say that the cardinality of [MATH: A] is (strictly) smaller than the cardinality of [MATH: B.]
> [MATH: |A| < |B|]

Content:
Following similar lines, we can also define [MATH: |A|\leq |B|{:}]

Content:
> If there exists an injection [MATH: f:A \to B] that maps [MATH: A] into [MATH: B,] we write
> [MATH: |A| \leq |B|.]

We can illustrate [MATH: |A|\leq |B|] for two (possibly infinite) sets [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] as follows:

Content:
In previous lessons, we saw that the cardinality of the natural numbers is [MATH: |\mathbb N| = \aleph_0,] the cardinality of the reals is [MATH: |\mathbb R| = \mathfrak{c},] and that these two cardinalities are different. We're now able to state that
[MATH: |\mathbb N| < |\mathbb R|.]
To see why, note the following:

Content:
- It's easy to find an injective function [MATH: f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R.] For example [MATH: f(n) = n] is injective.
- However, Cantor's diagonal argument shows no bijection exists between [MATH: \mathbb N] and [MATH: \mathbb R].
- Therefore, by definition, we have [MATH: |\mathbb N| < |\mathbb R|,] i.e.,
[MATH: \aleph_0 < \mathfrak{c}.]

Item 2 — Tutorial: The Cantor-Bernstein-Schröder Theorem

Content:
We're now able to discuss the main result of this lesson.

Content:
> If [MATH: |A| \leq |B|] and [MATH: |B| \leq |A|,] then [MATH: |A| = |B|.] In other words, if there exist injections [MATH: f:A \to B] and [MATH: g:B \to A,] then there exists a bijection [MATH: h] between [MATH: A] and [MATH: B.]

Content:
This theorem is known as the Cantor-Bernstein-Schröder theorem. It gives us a handy method of showing that two sets have the same cardinality without explicitly finding a bijection between them.

- The injection [MATH: g] maps [MATH: B] to [MATH: g(B),] where [MATH: g(B)\subseteq A.]

Item 10 — Tutorial: Proving the Existence of a Bijection Between a Square and an Interval

Content:
As an example of an application of the Cantor-Bernstein-Schröder theorem, let's prove that

Content:
[MATH: \big| (0,1) \times (0,1) \big| = \big| (0,1) \big| = \mathfrak{c}.]

Content:
Obviously, the function [MATH: f: x \to (x, 0.5)] for [MATH: x\in (0,1)] is an injection from [MATH: (0,1)] into [MATH: (0,1) \times (0,1).]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/36e78ab7f194381775a54a78621355b9]

Content:
Now, let's construct an injection from [MATH: (0,1) \times (0,1)] to [MATH: (0,1).]

Content:
Recall that

Content:
[MATH: (0,1) \times (0,1) = \{ (a,b) \mid a,b \in (0,1) \},]

Content:
and any real number from the interval [MATH: (0,1)] can be represented as a decimal with zero whole part. We will consider only the decimal representations that do not have repeating [MATH: 9]'s at the end. For example,
[MATH: 0.5=0.4\overline{9},]
but we take only the representation [MATH: 0.5.]

Content:
As a result, any element from [MATH: (0,1) \times (0,1)] can be uniquely represented by the decimal pair

Content:
[MATH: \big(0.a_1a_2a_3 \ldots, \: 0.b_1b_2b_3 \ldots \big).]

Content:
Next, let's define a function [MATH: g: (0,1) \times (0,1) \to (0,1)] that maps the above pair to the number

Content:
[MATH: 0.a_1b_1a_2b_2a_3b_3 \ldots]

Content:
This function is an injection since [MATH: g(x) \neq g(y)] whenever [MATH: x \neq y.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/cf26071700e67ecfd272f92b6f4b859f]

Content:
Therefore, according to the Cantor-Bernstein-Schröder theorem, we have that

Content:
[MATH: \big| (0,1) \times (0,1) \big| = \big| (0,1) \big|.]

Content:
Similarly, we can prove that
[MATH: \big| \mathbb{R}^2 \big| = \big| \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \big| = \big| \mathbb{R} \big| = \mathfrak{c}.]

Example Prompt:

> [MATH: g: (x,y) \to \bigg(x, \bbox[2pt, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAA}} \bigg)]
> is an injection from [MATH: \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}] onto [MATH: \mathbb{R} \times (-1,1) \subseteq \mathbb{R} \times [-2,3],] according to Cantor-Bernstein-Schröder theorem, we have that
> [MATH: \big| \mathbb{R} \times [-2,3] \big| = \bbox[2pt, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAA}}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
According to the Cantor-Bernstein-Schröder theorem, if [MATH: |A| \leq |B|] and [MATH: |B| \leq |A|,] then [MATH: |A| = |B|.]

In other words, if there exist injections [MATH: f: A \to B] and [MATH: g: B \to A,] then there exists a bijection between [MATH: A] and [MATH: B.]

With that in mind, we note the following:

- The function [MATH: f: (x,y) \to (x, y)] (that maps any ordered pair to itself) is an injection from [MATH: \mathbb{R} \times [-2,3]] into [MATH: \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}.] So, we have
[MATH: \big| \mathbb{R} \times [-2,3] \big| \leq \big| \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \big|.]
- On the other hand, the function
[MATH: x \to x]
injectively maps [MATH: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R},] and
[MATH: y \to \dfrac{2}{\pi}\arctan(y)]
injectively maps [MATH: \mathbb{R}] onto [MATH: (-1,1) \subseteq [-2,3].] Thus,
[MATH: g: (x,y) \to \bigg(x, \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\dfrac{2}{\pi}} \, \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\arctan(y)} \bigg)]
is an injection from [MATH: \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}] onto [MATH: \mathbb{R} \times (-1,1) \subseteq \mathbb{R} \times [-2,3],] as shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/6cf0f78c4e17a4223868f949a11c3411]

So, we have
[MATH: \big| \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \big| \leq \big| \mathbb{R} \times [-2,3]\big|.]

Therefore, by Cantor-Bernstein-Schröder theorem,

[MATH: \big| \mathbb{R} \times [-2,3] \big| = \big| \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \big| = \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\mathfrak{c}}.]
